intro: Every day you run into the same problem, even if you never call it by name. You want more time than the day holds. You want more things than your paycheck buys. Your school wants more teachers, laptops and repairs than its budget covers. Your city, your state and your country all want more than they can have. Economists call this problem scarcity, and it does not go away when people get richer. It is the starting point for everything in this course.

This unit gives you the basic tools economists use to think about scarcity. You will learn what goods are made from, the questions every economy must answer, and the different systems societies use to answer them. Then you will learn to measure what a choice really costs: the next-best alternative you give up, the hidden costs people forget, and the extra cost of one more hour or one more unit. You will see why sunk costs should be ignored and why people who specialize and trade end up with more.

By the end you will be able to name the opportunity cost in a real decision, read a production possibilities table, decide at the margin with numbers, and explain why two people who trade freely both come out ahead. Those skills work at a job, in a class schedule, in a family budget and in a debate about government policy.
bigQuestion: If we can never have everything we want, how should people and societies decide what to give up?

test.q: A store sells out of a new phone on launch day at $800. Which statement is correct?
choices: The phone became scarce only on launch day
The phone is a free good
Scarcity will end when the store restocks
There is a shortage at $800, and the phone is scarce as well
test.why: A shortage is a temporary gap at one price. Scarcity is permanent, because the phone always uses resources that could make something else.

test.q: A delivery van used by a bakery is which factor of production?
choices: Land
Capital
Labor
Entrepreneurship
test.why: Capital is a produced good used to make or deliver other goods. The van was built to help run the business.

test.q: A worker's output rises from 25 to 30 units an hour after training. What is the percent increase in productivity?
choices: 20 percent
5 percent
16.7 percent
30 percent
test.why: The gain is 5 units on a base of 25: 5 divided by 25 equals 0.20, or 20 percent. Dividing by 30 gives the wrong 16.7 percent.

test.q: In which economic system do prices set by buyers and sellers mainly decide what gets produced?
choices: Traditional
Command
Market
Feudal
test.why: In a market economy, prices signal what people want and give producers an incentive to supply it.

test.q: A city charges a fee for every plastic bag at checkout, and bag use falls. This is an example of
choices: central planning
a sunk cost
comparative advantage
a negative incentive
test.why: The fee is a small penalty that raises the cost of using a bag, so people use fewer. That is a negative incentive.

test.q: Which of these is a positive statement?
choices: Taxes on soda are unfair to poor families
A tax on soda reduced soda sales in the city that tried it
The city ought to tax soda
People should drink less soda
test.why: A positive statement can be checked against evidence. The other three are value judgments using words like unfair, ought and should.

test.q: Carlos turns down a job paying $500 a week to spend a week at a sports camp that costs $300. What does the camp cost him in dollars?
test.why: He pays $300 and gives up $500 in wages, so the full opportunity cost is $300 plus $500, or $800.

test.q: A shop owner earns $60,000 in accounting profit but could earn $70,000 managing another store. What is her economic profit?
test.why: Economic profit subtracts the implicit cost of her time: $60,000 minus $70,000 equals negative $10,000.

test.q: An economy can make 100 food and 0 tools, or 90 food and 10 tools, or 70 food and 20 tools. What happens to the cost of tools as more are made?
choices: It stays at 1 food per tool
It falls from 2 to 1 food per tool
It rises from 1 to 2 food per tool
Tools have no cost because food is plentiful
test.why: The first 10 tools cost 10 food, or 1 each. The next 10 cost 20 food, or 2 each. That is the law of increasing opportunity cost.

test.q: Which of these is an example of economic growth on a PPC?
choices: Hiring back workers laid off in a recession
A new technology that lets farms and factories produce more
Choosing to make more food and fewer tools
A drought that destroys part of the harvest
test.why: Better technology raises the most an economy can produce, shifting the whole curve outward. Rehiring idle workers only moves toward the curve.

test.q: A movie theater gets $300 in extra ticket sales from a late show that costs $250 to run, and $180 from a second late show that also costs $250. How many late shows should it run?
choices: Only the second one
test.why: The first show's marginal benefit, $300, is above its $250 cost. The second show's $180 is below $250, so the theater should run just one.

test.q: A city has spent $5 million on a stadium plan. Finishing it will cost $20 million more and bring $15 million in benefits. What should the city weigh?
choices: The $20 million cost against the $15 million benefit
The $5 million already spent against the $15 million benefit
The full $25 million against the $15 million benefit
Nothing, because the plan is already started
test.why: The $5 million is sunk. Looking forward, $20 million in cost for $15 million in benefit is a bad deal, whatever was spent before.

test.q: In an hour, Kim can type 10 pages or answer 20 emails, and Leo can type 4 pages or answer 16 emails. Who has the comparative advantage in answering emails?
choices: Kim, because she answers more emails per hour
Neither of them
Leo, because an email costs him a quarter of a page and costs Kim half a page
Kim, because she is faster at both
test.why: For Kim an email costs 10 divided by 20, or 0.5 pages. For Leo it costs 4 divided by 16, or 0.25 pages. Leo gives up less.

test.q: A buyer who values a used guitar at $250 pays the seller $180, and the seller would have taken $120. What are the total gains from trade?
test.why: The buyer gains $250 minus $180, or $70. The seller gains $180 minus $120, or $60. Together they gain $130.

test.q: Why do economists describe the United States as a mixed economy?
choices: Most prices are set by government officials
Its economy runs mainly on tradition
It trades with many other countries
Private markets produce most goods while government also produces, regulates and taxes
test.why: The mix is between markets and government. Private firms make most things, and government runs schools, roads and courts and sets rules.

write.prompt: A friend has been offered a paid summer internship ($3,000 for 10 weeks) and also a spot on a travel sports team that costs $1,200. Using the unit's tools, decide which she should choose. Show the opportunity cost of each option in dollars, name any sunk or nonmonetary costs, and argue your conclusion.
tips: Name the single next-best alternative for each option, not a list.
Show your numbers: add explicit costs and forgone earnings for each choice.
Leave out any money already spent that cannot be recovered.
Name at least one benefit or cost that has no price tag and say how much it weighs.
End with a clear choice and the trade-off she accepts by making it.

title: Scarcity, Choice and Opportunity Cost

chapters.title: Scarcity Is Not a Shortage
chapters.bigQuestion: If there will never be enough of everything for everyone, how does a society decide who gets what?

story.title: Twenty-Four Hours
story.kicker: On a Sunday night a Chicago junior adds up everything she wants to do on Monday and discovers the day is seven hours short.
paragraphs: Maya sat on her bed with a notebook and wrote down Monday. School, seven hours. Sleep, nine, because the coach said so. Her shift at the grocery store on Pulaski, four hours. Soccer practice, two. Homework for chemistry and history, three. Dinner with her family, one. A movie her friends had been planning for two weeks, three hours with the ride. Guitar, which she had promised herself she would finally start, one hour. Then she added the column. Thirty-one hours.

The day has twenty-four. Maya started cutting. The movie went first, and she felt it go. Then she cut sleep to seven hours and knew she would pay for that at practice. Guitar went back on the someday list, where it had lived since eighth grade. Even after all that, she was still an hour over, so homework became two hours and history would get skimmed. Every line she crossed out was something she really wanted.

Her cousin Dani, home from college, looked over her shoulder and laughed. Welcome to economics, she said. Maya said she was just bad at planning. Dani shook her head. The problem was not the planning. The problem was that Maya wanted thirty-one hours of things and had twenty-four hours to want them in. That would be true tomorrow too, and it would be true if Maya were rich, famous or the governor of Illinois. Nobody can buy a twenty-fifth hour.

Dani pointed out that the same thing was happening everywhere at bigger scales. The school board downtown was choosing that week between fixing a roof and buying laptops, with money that could not do both. A farm near Bloomington was deciding how many acres to plant in corn and how many in soybeans. The state legislature was arguing over a budget in which every dollar spent on roads was a dollar not spent on something else.

Maya looked at her crossed-out list. She had not solved the problem, because it cannot be solved. She had answered it, for one day, by choosing. This chapter is about that problem, why it never goes away, and the very different ways that people, businesses and whole countries answer it.
story.think: Maya cannot buy more hours. Which item on her list would you have cut first, and what rule did you use to decide?

lessons.title: Wants Outrun Resources
lessons.mainIdea: Scarcity means that wants are unlimited while the resources to satisfy them are limited, so every person and every society must choose.
reading: Picture a $40 gift card to a store you like. You walk in wanting headphones at $35, a hoodie at $30 and sneakers at $60. Your *wants* add up to $125 and the card holds $40. Now imagine a relative hands you a second card worth $200. You can buy all three items, but on the way to the register you notice concert tickets at $90 and a jacket at $120. The list of things you want did not close. It grew to fit the new money.

That is *scarcity*: the condition in which people want more than the available *resources* can provide. Scarcity is not the same as being poor. A student with $40 and a company with $40 billion both face it, because wants expand faster than means. Time makes the point most clearly. Every person on Earth, rich or poor, gets the same 24 hours a day, and almost everyone wants more from those hours than they can hold.

*Economics* is the study of how people choose to use scarce resources to satisfy their wants. Economists study those choices at two scales. Microeconomics looks at individual households, businesses and markets, such as how a bakery sets its prices. Macroeconomics looks at the whole economy, such as why unemployment rises in a recession. This unit begins where all of it begins, with the fact that choices must be made.

The most important consequence of scarcity is choice. Because you cannot have everything, picking one thing means not picking another. Maya could not fit the movie and nine hours of sleep into the same night. A city cannot put the same $200,000 into both a park and a fire truck. The next chapter measures exactly what a choice costs. This chapter asks a bigger question first: since everyone must choose, who decides, and how?

the goods, services and experiences people would like to have, which keep growing as means grow

the study of how people choose to use scarce resources to satisfy their wants

look.title: The $40 Card
look.text: You have a $40 gift card. The store has headphones for $35, a hoodie for $30, a phone case for $12, a water bottle for $18 and sneakers for $60. You can only spend the $40 today, and there is no way to add to it.
look.prompt: Which items do you buy, what do you leave behind, and would your answer change if the card were worth $100? What happened to your list of wants when the card grew?

check.q: Which situation best shows scarcity as economists define it?
choices: A student with a $40 gift card who wants $125 worth of items
A store that runs out of headphones for one afternoon
A family with more food in the freezer than it can eat
A country that has no gold mines
check.why: Scarcity is wants greater than the means to satisfy them. The student wants more than $40 can buy, and that will stay true even if the card grows.

check.q: Why does scarcity still apply to a billionaire?
choices: Because money loses value every year
Because wants grow as means grow, and no one can buy more than 24 hours in a day
Because billionaires must pay higher taxes
It does not; scarcity only applies to people with low incomes
check.why: Scarcity is about the gap between wants and means, not about being poor. Wants expand to fit new money, and time is limited for everyone.

check.q: Economics is best described as the study of
choices: how to get rich quickly
how governments print money
how people choose to use limited resources to satisfy their wants
how businesses design advertisements
check.why: The standard definition centers on choice under scarcity. Money, government and business are all part of it, but choice is the core.

lessons.title: Scarcity Is Not a Shortage
lessons.mainIdea: A shortage is temporary and exists at a particular price; scarcity is permanent and applies to almost every good.
reading: A popular game console launches at $500 in November. Stores sell out in hours, and people who wanted one walk away empty-handed. Twelve weeks later the same console sits on the shelf at the same $500, and anyone who wants one can buy it. In November there was a *shortage*: at the going price, the *quantity demanded* by buyers was larger than the *quantity supplied* by sellers. By February the shortage was gone.

Put numbers on it. Suppose that at $500, buyers wanted 1,000,000 consoles in launch week, but the maker could ship only 600,000. The shortage was 1,000,000 minus 600,000, or 400,000 consoles. By week twelve the factories had caught up and shipped 1,000,000, so quantity supplied matched quantity demanded. A shortage ends when supply catches up or when the price rises enough that fewer people want to buy.

Scarcity did not end in February. The console was still scarce, because making each one used up chips, plastic, factory time and workers that could have made something else. Here is the test: if the price were zero, would people want more of it than exists? For consoles, yes. For almost everything, yes. Scarcity is the permanent gap between wants and resources. A shortage is a temporary gap between what buyers want and what sellers offer at one particular price.

The difference matters because the two problems have different fixes. A shortage can be fixed by producing more or by letting the price rise. Scarcity cannot be fixed at all; it can only be managed by choosing well. Watch the news for the word shortage. A drought that cuts a town's water supply creates a real shortage at the current water rates. But water was scarce before the drought and will be scarce in a wet year too, because it is never free to collect, clean and deliver.

words.d: a situation in which buyers want more of a good than sellers offer at the current price
the amount of a good buyers are willing and able to buy at a particular price
the amount of a good sellers are willing and able to sell at a particular price

look.title: A Console Launch (example)
look.cite: Made-up figures for a game console launch, used to show a shortage
look.prompt: In which week is there a shortage, and how large is it? Is the console scarce in week 12? Explain the difference in one sentence.

check.q: At $500, buyers want 1,000,000 consoles and sellers ship 600,000. How large is the shortage?
choices: 1,600,000 consoles
600,000 consoles
1,000,000 consoles
400,000 consoles
check.why: A shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied at the current price: 1,000,000 minus 600,000 equals 400,000.

check.q: Which statement is true once the console sits on shelves at $500 with no one turned away?
choices: The console is no longer scarce
The console has become a free good
The console is still scarce but no longer in shortage
The shortage will return every year at the same time
check.why: The shortage ended when supply caught up. Scarcity remains, because the console still uses resources that could have made something else.

check.q: A drought cuts a town's water supply, and at the usual rates people want more water than the town can deliver. Which description is best?
choices: Water became scarce for the first time
Water was always scarce, and now there is also a shortage at the current price
Water is a free good, so this is neither a shortage nor scarcity
The drought created scarcity, which will end when the rain returns
check.why: Scarcity is permanent, because water always takes resources to deliver. The drought added a temporary shortage at the going price.

lessons.title: No Such Thing as a Free Lunch
lessons.mainIdea: Almost every good uses scarce resources, so someone pays for it even when the price to you is zero.
reading: A club at school offers free pizza at its Thursday meeting. To you the price is zero. Look closer. The club paid $60 out of its dues. The pizza shop used flour, cheese, an oven and a worker's time. You spent thirty minutes in a room you might have spent somewhere else. The pizza was free to you, but it was not free. Someone paid in money, and everyone paid in resources that could have gone to another use.

Economists sort goods into two piles. A *free good* is one that exists in greater quantity than people want even at a price of zero, so nobody has to give anything up to get more of it. Sunlight on a farm field and the air you breathe outdoors are the standard examples. An *economic good* is scarce: getting more of it requires giving something up. Nearly everything you can name, from pencils to public schools, is an economic good. Illinois spends thousands of dollars per student each year to run its public schools, all of it raised through taxes.

Try it with numbers. A city announces that it will give away 5,000 free shade trees to residents. Each tree costs $40 to grow, deliver and plant. The program costs 5,000 times $40, or $200,000, paid from the city budget. That $200,000 is not available for road repair, library hours or a tax cut. The trees may be a wonderful use of the money. They are still not free. The *cost* simply landed somewhere other than the person taking the tree home.

Asking who really pays, and what was given up, is the first habit of economic thinking. It does not mean free lunches are bad. Free school meals, free concerts in Millennium Park and free clinics can be worth every dollar. It means the dollars exist and came from somewhere. When a program is called free, an economist hears a question: free to whom, and paid for by whom?

words.d: a good so plentiful that people can have all they want at no cost, such as sunlight
a scarce good; getting more of it means giving something else up
what must be given up to get something, whether money, time or another good

look.title: The Free Concert
look.text: A city offers a free outdoor concert in a downtown park. There is no ticket. The stage rental costs $30,000, the band is paid $50,000, and police and cleanup crews cost $20,000. About 20,000 people attend, and many of them buy dinner nearby afterward.
look.prompt: Who pays for the concert, and roughly how much per attendee? List two things the city gave up to hold it, and one reason it might still be a good choice.

check.q: Which of these is a free good in the economic sense?
choices: A free sample handed out at a grocery store
A library book you borrow at no charge
Sunlight falling on a farm field
A free outdoor concert
check.why: A free good exists in greater quantity than anyone wants at a zero price. The sample, the book and the concert all used scarce resources that someone paid for.

check.q: A city gives away 5,000 trees that cost $40 each to grow and plant. What does the program cost the city budget?
check.why: 5,000 trees times $40 per tree equals $200,000. That money is no longer available for other city needs.

check.q: The saying that there is no free lunch means
choices: nobody should ever give things away
every good that uses scarce resources is paid for by someone
free meals are against the rules in most places
lunch always costs more than breakfast
check.why: The saying is about cost, not policy. A gift can be a good idea, but its resources came from somewhere and could have been used for something else.

lessons.title: Land and Labor
lessons.mainIdea: Every good is made from four kinds of resources called the factors of production; land and labor are the first two.
reading: Follow a loaf of bread backward from a Chicago bakery. The flour came from wheat that grew in soil, drank rain and soaked up sunlight. A farmer planted and harvested it, a mill ground it, a truck driver hauled it, and a baker mixed and shaped it before dawn. Economists group everything used to make the loaf into four categories called the *factors of production*: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. This lesson covers the first two.

*Land* means every natural resource, not just dirt. It includes soil, water, minerals, timber, oil, wind and the fish in Lake Michigan. Illinois is rich in this factor. Its deep prairie soil is among the most productive in the world, and the state is one of the nation's leading producers of corn and soybeans. Land earns a payment called rent. A landowner who lets a farmer use 100 acres is renting out a factor of production.

*Labor* means human effort, both physical and mental. The farmer, the truck driver, the baker, a nurse, a software developer and a teacher are all supplying labor. Its payment is wages. Labor has quantity, meaning workers times hours, and quality. The quality part is called *human capital*: the skills, knowledge and health a worker brings to the job. Two bakers can share the same oven, yet a trained baker turns out 80 loaves in a shift while a beginner turns out 50. That extra 30 loaves is a 60 percent gain, and it came entirely from human capital.

Countries and regions differ in which factors they have. Illinois has abundant farmland and a large, skilled workforce clustered around Chicago. A small island nation may have little land but plenty of labor. Economists ask which factor is scarce in a place, because that shapes what the place produces and what it trades for. A region does not need to have every factor. It needs to use the ones it has well.

words.d: the four kinds of resources used to make goods and services: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship
all natural resources used in production, including soil, water, minerals and energy sources
the physical and mental effort people supply to produce goods and services
the skills, knowledge and health that make a worker more productive

look.title: Follow the Loaf
look.text: A loaf of bread reaches a Chicago shelf. Behind it are rain on a wheat field, a combine harvester, a farmer's early mornings, a rail car, a mill worker, natural gas for the oven, the baker's ten years of practice, and the owner who borrowed money to open the shop.
look.prompt: Sort each item into land or labor. Which items do not fit either category? Those belong to the two factors in the next lesson.

check.q: Which of these counts as land in the economist's sense?
choices: A tractor
A farm worker
A farm's bank loan
Iron ore in a mine
check.why: Land means natural resources of every kind, including minerals underground. A tractor is capital, a worker is labor, and a loan is money, not a factor.

check.q: A trained baker makes 80 loaves per shift and a beginner makes 50 with the same oven. By what percent does training raise output?
choices: 30 percent
37.5 percent
60 percent
160 percent
check.why: The gain is 30 loaves on a base of 50: 30 divided by 50 equals 0.60, or 60 percent. Dividing by 80 instead gives the wrong 37.5 percent.

check.q: Human capital is best described as
choices: the skills, knowledge and health workers bring to a job
the money a worker keeps in savings
machines that replace workers
the number of workers in a country
check.why: Human capital is the quality of labor. It is built by education, training and good health, and it raises what a worker can produce in an hour.

lessons.title: Capital and Entrepreneurship
lessons.mainIdea: Capital is the tools and buildings made to produce other things, and entrepreneurs are the people who combine all the factors and take the risk.
reading: Back in the bakery, look at what the baker uses: an oven, two mixers, a walk-in cooler, a delivery van and the building itself. Economists call these *capital*: goods that were produced in order to produce other goods and services. Here is a common mistake. In everyday talk, capital means money. In economics, the $6,000 the baker spent is not capital; the mixer she bought with it is. Money buys factors of production, but money itself bakes nothing.

Capital matters because it raises *productivity*, the amount of output a worker produces in an hour. Suppose the baker kneads by hand and makes 40 loaves a day. She buys a $6,000 mixer and now makes 120 loaves a day with the same hours. Output tripled, a rise of 200 percent. Notice that the mixer was itself made from steel, wire and labor. Someone had to give up making consumer goods to make that machine. A society builds capital by saving, which means not consuming everything it produces today.

The fourth factor is the person who put the bakery together. An *entrepreneur* has an idea, gathers land, labor and capital, and takes the risk that the idea will fail. The baker signed a lease, borrowed $6,000, hired two workers and opened the doors without knowing whether anyone would buy her bread. If they do not, she loses her savings. If they do, she earns *profit*, the money left after all costs are paid. Profit is the reward for taking that risk, and the chance of loss is what makes it a risk.

Put the four factors together with the payment each one earns. Land earns rent. Labor earns wages. Capital earns interest, the payment for the use of saved money and the machines it buys. Entrepreneurship earns profit. Every business on every block in Chicago, from a corner taqueria to a steel plant, combines these four. How much of each a country has, and how well it combines them, decides how much that country can produce.

words.d: goods that were produced to make other goods and services, such as tools, machines and buildings
the amount of output produced per worker per hour, or per unit of any input
a person who organizes land, labor and capital to produce something and accepts the risk of loss
the money a business has left after paying all of its costs

look.title: One Bakery, Three Setups (example)
rows: With the mixer and a second oven
look.cite: Made-up figures for one bakery with the same two workers in each setup
look.prompt: How many extra loaves did the mixer add? How many did the second oven add? Which piece of capital raised productivity more, and what would you want to know before buying the oven?

check.q: Which of these is capital in the economist's sense?
choices: $6,000 in a savings account
A bakery's dough mixer
The baker's ten years of skill
The wheat in the flour
check.why: Capital is a produced good used to make other goods. The money is financial, the skill is human capital, and the wheat is a raw material from land.

check.q: Output rose from 40 loaves a day to 120 after a mixer was installed. Which describes the change?
choices: It rose by 80 percent
It doubled
It rose by 300 percent
It tripled, a rise of 200 percent
check.why: 120 divided by 40 equals 3, so output tripled. The increase is 80 loaves on a base of 40, which is 200 percent, not 300.

check.q: What separates an entrepreneur from an employee of the same business?
choices: Entrepreneurs never do physical work
Entrepreneurs take the risk of loss in order to organize production
Entrepreneurs must own the land the business sits on
Entrepreneurs are paid a fixed wage each week
check.why: The defining feature is risk. The entrepreneur combines the other factors and keeps the profit if it works, or absorbs the loss if it does not.

lessons.title: More From the Same
lessons.mainIdea: Productivity is output per unit of input; raising it is the main way a society gets more from the same scarce resources.
reading: Stand on one acre of Illinois farmland. In the 1930s that acre produced roughly 30 bushels of corn in a good year. Today the same acre often produces close to 200. The soil did not get bigger. What changed was everything applied to it: hybrid seed, tractors and combines, fertilizer, drainage, weather data and three generations of farming knowledge. Those are capital, human capital and *technology*, and together they multiplied what one acre can do.

This is productivity at work. Productivity is output per unit of input, usually measured per worker per hour or per acre. Compare two sandwich stations in a cafe. At station A a worker makes 12 sandwiches an hour. At station B, with a better layout and a faster press, a worker makes 20. With two workers on eight-hour shifts, station A yields 2 times 8 times 12, or 192 sandwiches a day. Station B yields 2 times 8 times 20, or 320. Same workers, same hours, 128 more sandwiches.

Where does higher productivity come from? From more and better capital, from human capital built by education and training, from technology, meaning better knowledge of how to combine inputs, and from specialization, which the next chapter explains. Each source has a price. Building the better sandwich station means spending money now that could have bought other things. That is *investment*: giving up some consumption today to produce more tomorrow.

Over decades, productivity growth is the main reason a country's *standard of living* rises. When each hour of work produces more, there is more to go around, whether it is paid out as higher wages, lower prices or more free time. A common mistake is to confuse productivity with effort. Working longer hours at the same pace raises total output but not productivity. Working with better tools, skills and methods raises both.

words.d: knowledge of how to combine inputs to produce goods and services, including new methods and machines
spending on capital goods now in order to produce more in the future
the amount of goods and services the average person in a place can consume

look.title: Two Sandwich Stations
look.text: A cafe owner can rebuild her sandwich station for $4,000. Each of her two workers would go from 12 sandwiches an hour to 20. She sells every sandwich she makes at $8, and each one costs $3 in ingredients. She is open eight hours a day.
look.prompt: How many extra sandwiches per day does the new station produce, and how much extra money is that per day after ingredients? About how many days until the $4,000 pays for itself?

check.q: Station A makes 12 sandwiches per worker-hour and station B makes 20. With two workers on eight-hour shifts, how many more sandwiches does B produce per day?
check.why: Station A: 2 workers times 8 hours times 12 equals 192. Station B: 2 times 8 times 20 equals 320. The difference is 128.

check.q: An acre of Illinois farmland that gave roughly 30 bushels of corn in the 1930s now gives close to 200. What best explains the change?
choices: Better seed, machines and knowledge applied to the same land
The acre grew larger over time
The sun became brighter over Illinois
Farmers began working more hours per day
check.why: The land is fixed. Capital, human capital and technology raised the output per acre, which is what productivity growth means.

check.q: Which of these raises productivity rather than just total output?
choices: Working longer hours at the same pace
Hiring more workers who use the same tools
Paying workers less per hour
Giving workers a faster tool and training to use it
check.why: Productivity is output per hour of work. Only better tools, skills or methods raise it. More hours or more workers raise total output without changing output per hour.

lessons.title: What, How and for Whom
lessons.mainIdea: Because of scarcity, every economy must answer three questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and who gets it.
reading: A high school receives a $50,000 grant. The principal faces three decisions in a row. First, what should the money become: 250 laptops at $200 each, or a new weight room? Second, how should the work be done: hire an outside contractor or have the district's own staff install everything? Third, if it is laptops, who gets them: seniors first, one per classroom, or a lottery? Every economy, from a village to the United States, must answer those same three questions.

The first question is what to produce. Resources that go into one good cannot go into another, so a society must decide how much food, housing, health care, entertainment and defense it will make. The second is how to produce it. A field can be harvested by 40 workers with hand tools or by one worker with a combine. A car can be welded by people or by robots. Each method uses a different mix of the factors of *production*.

The third question is for whom. Once goods exist, some rule decides their *distribution*, meaning who ends up with them. Goods can go to whoever pays the most, to whoever waits in line longest, to whoever the government chooses, to whoever is related to the right people, or to everyone equally. Each rule rewards different behavior and feels fair to different people. This is the question where economics meets values most directly.

The way a society organizes its answers is its *economic system*. Some societies answer by custom, doing what their grandparents did. Some answer through a central authority that gives orders. Some answer through millions of separate buyers and sellers who never meet, guided by prices. Almost every real country mixes these. The next two lessons walk through each system, what it does well and what it does badly.

words.d: the way a society organizes the answers to what, how and for whom to produce
the process of combining resources to make goods and services
how the goods and services a society produces are divided among its people

look.title: The $50,000 Decision
look.text: Your school has a one-time $50,000 grant. Options: 250 laptops at $200 each; a weight room at $50,000; or 125 laptops plus a $25,000 upgrade to the science labs. Installation can be done by district staff over the summer or by a contractor in one week for $5,000 extra.
look.prompt: Answer the three questions: what, how and for whom. Give one reason for each answer and name one group that would be unhappy with your choice.

check.q: Choosing between 250 laptops and a weight room answers which economic question?
choices: For whom to produce
What to produce
How to produce
Where to produce
check.why: Deciding which goods the resources will become is the what question. How and for whom come after that choice.

check.q: A car company decides to weld its cars with robots instead of workers. Which question is it answering?
choices: What to produce
For whom to produce
Where to produce
How to produce
check.why: The company already knows it is making cars. Choosing the mix of capital and labor used to make them is the how question.

check.q: A city decides that only families below a certain income can receive free transit passes. Which question is that?
choices: For whom to produce
What to produce
How to produce
When to produce
check.why: The passes already exist. Deciding who receives them is the distribution question, for whom.

lessons.title: Tradition and Command
lessons.mainIdea: A traditional economy answers the three questions by custom; a command economy answers them through a central authority that plans and gives orders.
reading: In a *traditional economy*, the three questions are answered the way they were answered last year and the century before. A family farms because its parents farmed, plants the same crops, and shares the harvest by rules of kinship and custom. Everyone knows their role, and there are few surprises. The costs are just as clear. Output stays low, new ideas are slow to spread, and a bad harvest can be a disaster. Pure traditional economies are rare today, but custom still shapes some choices in every society.

In a *command economy*, a central authority, usually the government, owns most of the factors of production and decides what, how and for whom. The Soviet Union ran on *central planning* for most of the twentieth century. Planners in Moscow set targets in five-year plans, such as a certain number of tons of steel or pairs of shoes, and factories were ordered to meet them. Prices were set by decree rather than by buyers and sellers.

Command systems have a real strength: they can point a whole nation's resources at one goal quickly, as in wartime. Their weaknesses show up in daily life. Imagine a planner who must order shoes for 1,000,000 people. He knows the average foot is size 9, so he orders 1,000,000 pairs of size 9. People with size 7 feet line up for hours and go home empty-handed while size 9 piles up in warehouses. No planner can know what millions of people want, and a set price cannot signal when he guesses wrong. Workers and managers who are paid the same whether the shoes fit or not have little reason to fix it.

Today only a few countries, such as North Korea, come close to a pure command economy. Cuba keeps much of its economy under state control. China combines strong state direction of major industries with markets in much of daily life. Every economy that has tried to plan everything from the center has run into the same two problems: not enough information and not enough incentive. The next lesson turns to the system that tries to solve both.

words.d: an economic system in which custom and habit decide what, how and for whom to produce
an economic system in which a central authority owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom
the practice of having government officials set production targets and prices for the whole economy

look.title: The Shoe Plan
look.text: You are a planner ordering next year's shoes for a city of 1,000,000 people. You know last year's total, the average shoe size and how much leather the tannery can deliver. You do not know who wants boots, who wants sneakers, whose feet are growing or which styles will be popular by spring.
look.prompt: What information would you need to get the order right, and how would you collect it? What happens to the people whose sizes and styles you guess wrong?

check.q: In a traditional economy, what mainly decides how goods are produced?
choices: Government planners
Prices set by buyers and sellers
Custom and the way things were done before
A vote of all citizens
check.why: Tradition answers the three questions by habit and inherited roles, not by planners or by markets.

check.q: According to the reading, what is the central weakness of planning from the center?
choices: Planners always choose the wrong goals
Planners cannot know what millions of people want, and fixed prices cannot signal their mistakes
Command economies have too many businesses
Planning is against the law in most countries
check.why: The shoe example shows the information problem. Even a careful planner cannot gather the knowledge that millions of separate choices contain.

check.q: Which of these is a strength of a command economy?
choices: It produces the widest variety of consumer goods
It rewards workers who satisfy customers
It always sets prices at the right level
It can direct a nation's resources toward one big goal quickly
check.why: Central control makes it possible to move resources fast toward a single purpose, such as a war effort. The trade-off is weak information and incentives elsewhere.

lessons.title: Markets and Mixed Economies
lessons.mainIdea: A market economy answers the three questions through prices set by buyers and sellers; every real economy, including the United States, is a mix.
reading: Nobody in Chicago planned how many pizzas the city would make tonight. No office assigned the cheese, scheduled the drivers or decided which neighborhoods get deep dish. Yet tonight there will be pizza almost everywhere it is wanted, at prices people will pay. That is a *market economy*: households and businesses that own their own property make their own choices, trade with each other voluntarily, and are coordinated by prices rather than by orders.

Prices do the coordinating. Suppose a new pizza topping becomes popular and shops that offer it can charge $16 instead of $14 a pie. The higher price is a signal that people want more, and an incentive to supply it. More shops add the topping, suppliers grow more of the ingredient, and the price settles back. Adam Smith described this in 1776 as an *invisible hand*: each person seeks their own gain, and the result is goods reaching the people who want them, without anyone directing the whole. The system rests on *private property*, *voluntary exchange*, competition and the profit motive.

No country runs on markets alone. The United States is a *mixed economy*. Private businesses produce most goods and services, but government at every level builds roads, runs public schools, operates courts and the military, regulates food and drug safety, and collects taxes to pay for it all. Government spending at all levels in the United States adds up to roughly a third of the economy's output. Illinois runs public universities and the tollway system while private firms run nearly everything else. Countries differ in the mix, from more market-based to more government-directed, but every one is somewhere in between.

Markets have clear strengths: they use dispersed information, reward efficiency and drive innovation. They also have limits that later chapters examine, including pollution that no price captures, goods like national defense that no business can sell, and periods of high unemployment. Economists broadly agree that markets do most things well. They disagree, often sharply, about how much government should do around the edges. Both the agreement and the disagreement are part of the subject.

words.d: an economic system in which prices set by buyers and sellers answer what, how and for whom
an economy that combines private markets with government production, regulation and taxes; every real economy is one
the right of individuals and businesses to own, use and sell resources and goods
a trade that both sides agree to because each expects to be better off
Adam Smith's image for the way self-interested choices in a market end up serving other people

look.title: The Butcher, the Brewer and the Baker
look.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 2, 1776
look.prompt: According to Smith, why does the baker get up at 4 a.m. to make your bread? How does that connect to the way a market answers the question of what to produce?

check.q: In a market economy, what mainly answers the question of what to produce?
choices: Prices formed by the choices of buyers and sellers
Instructions from a planning office
Rules handed down by custom
A yearly vote by consumers
check.why: Prices signal what people want and give sellers an incentive to supply it. No central office is needed.

check.q: Why do economists call the United States a mixed economy?
choices: Because it uses several different currencies
Because half of all businesses are owned by the government
Because private firms produce most goods while government provides some goods and sets the rules
Because it mixes tradition with central planning
check.why: Markets do most of the producing, but government builds roads, runs schools and courts, regulates and taxes. That combination is the mix.

check.q: What is Adam Smith's point in the passage about the butcher, the brewer and the baker?
choices: Business owners are selfish and should be regulated
People serve others' needs while pursuing their own interest
Dinner should be provided by the government
Only kind people succeed in business
check.why: Smith's invisible hand: the baker feeds you because it pays him to, and the result is that you get bread without anyone planning it.

lessons.title: Incentives Matter
lessons.mainIdea: An incentive is a reward or penalty that changes behavior; economists predict that people respond to incentives, sometimes in ways nobody intended.
reading: A coffee shop near a high school starts a punch card: buy nine drinks, get the tenth free. Within a month a typical regular goes from two visits a week to three, a 50 percent increase. Across town a library charges 25 cents a day for late books, and more books come back on time. The punch card is a positive *incentive*, a reward for doing something. The fine is a negative incentive, a penalty for doing something. Both changed behavior without anyone giving an order.

Incentives come in many forms: money, time, grades, praise, convenience, the fear of a penalty. Prices are incentives, which is why markets work. Taxes and subsidies are incentives that governments design on purpose. A *subsidy* is a payment that lowers the cost of doing something, such as a tax credit for installing solar panels. A tax raises the cost. In 2017 Chicago began charging a 7-cent fee on each paper or plastic checkout bag, and shoppers quickly began bringing their own bags. Seven cents was enough to change millions of small decisions.

Incentives also produce surprises. A school offers students a prize for every book they read. Reading goes up, but the books get shorter and thinner, because the prize rewards the number of books, not the amount of reading. That is an *unintended consequence*: a result the designer of the incentive did not want and did not expect. It happened because people responded to the rule exactly as written rather than to the goal behind it.

So when any rule, price or policy changes, an economist asks three questions. Who gains? Who loses? How will each of them change what they do? The answers predict behavior better than good intentions do. A policy that assumes people will ignore an incentive is usually a policy that will not work as planned.

words.d: a reward or penalty that encourages or discourages a particular choice
a government payment or tax break that lowers the cost of producing or buying something
an outcome of a rule or incentive that the people who designed it did not intend

look.title: The Per-Book Prize
look.text: A middle school offers a $5 gift card for every book a student finishes, with no rules about length. In the first month the number of books read doubles, but the librarian notices that the average book checked out drops from 220 pages to 90 pages, and some students finish three picture books in an afternoon.
look.prompt: What did the incentive actually reward? Rewrite the rule so it rewards what the school wanted, and name one new problem your version might create.

check.q: Chicago's 7-cent fee on each checkout bag is an example of
choices: a subsidy
a positive incentive
a free good
a negative incentive
check.why: The fee is a small penalty attached to using a bag. It raises the cost of the behavior, which is what a negative incentive does.

check.q: Students paid per book start choosing very short books. This best illustrates
choices: a shortage of long books
an unintended consequence of an incentive
the invisible hand
the law of increasing opportunity cost
check.why: The rule rewarded the count of books, so students responded to the count. The designers wanted more reading and got something different.

check.q: A regular customer goes from 2 visits a week to 3 after a punch card starts. What is the percent increase?
choices: 50 percent
33 percent
100 percent
150 percent
check.why: The increase is 1 visit on a base of 2: 1 divided by 2 equals 0.50, or 50 percent. Dividing by 3 gives the wrong 33 percent.

lessons.title: The Economic Way of Thinking
lessons.mainIdea: Economists assume people weigh costs and benefits, build simple models to isolate one cause at a time, and separate what is from what ought to be.
reading: You hold a $60 concert ticket for Saturday. Friday afternoon your manager offers you a Saturday shift at time and a half, worth $150. Notice what an economist assumes about you. You will act purposefully, comparing the pleasure of the concert against the $150 and choosing the one you value more. Economists call this being *rational*, which does not mean cold or greedy. It means people pursue their own goals, whatever those goals are, and respond when costs and benefits change.

Economists also build models. A *model* is a simplified picture of how something works, like a subway map that leaves out every street to show the lines clearly. The most useful modeling tool has a Latin name, *ceteris paribus*, which means other things being equal. To see the effect of one cause, hold everything else constant. If gas prices rise 10 percent, people buy less gas, other things equal. In the real world incomes, weather and car sales are all changing too, so the model isolates one thread at a time.

Finally, economists separate two kinds of statements. A *positive statement* describes how the world is and can be tested against evidence: raising a city's minimum wage will change teen employment by some measurable amount. A *normative statement* says how the world ought to be: the minimum wage should be higher. Positive statements can be wrong; normative statements rest on values. Economists tend to agree much more about positive questions than about normative ones, and a good argument keeps the two apart.

Put the habits together and you have the economic way of thinking. Everything has a cost. People respond to incentives. Decisions happen one step at a time, at the margin, which the next chapter explains. Simple models beat no model. And when you hear an argument about the economy, ask whether it is a claim about facts or a claim about values. The rest of this course is practice in those five habits.

words.d: acting purposefully to reach your own goals by weighing costs and benefits
a simplified description of how part of the economy works, used to make predictions
other things being equal; holding everything else constant to study one cause
a claim about how the world is that can be tested against evidence
a claim about how the world ought to be, based on values

look.title: A Definition That Stuck
look.text: In 1932 the British economist Lionel Robbins defined economics as the study of human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses. Most textbooks still open with a version of that sentence.
look.cite: Lionel Robbins, An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science, 1932 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Robbins names three things: ends, scarce means and alternative uses. Match each one to something in Maya's Monday from the chapter story.

check.q: Which of these is a positive statement?
choices: Gasoline should be cheaper than it is
The government ought to tax gasoline more heavily
A $1 rise in the price of gasoline reduces the amount bought by about 3 percent
Wealthy people deserve to pay more for gasoline
check.why: A positive statement can be tested against data. The other three use should, ought and deserve, which signal value judgments.

check.q: Ceteris paribus means
choices: the more the better
let the buyer beware
everything changes at once
holding other factors constant
check.why: The phrase means other things being equal. It lets a model study one cause while everything else is held still.

check.q: Studying how a single bakery decides what price to charge belongs to
choices: macroeconomics
microeconomics
normative economics
central planning
check.why: Microeconomics studies individual households, businesses and markets. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole.

review.q: Which statement best explains why scarcity can never be eliminated?
choices: Wants keep growing as resources grow, and time is fixed for everyone
Governments refuse to print enough money
Most countries lack natural resources
Factories cannot run 24 hours a day
review.why: Scarcity is the permanent gap between unlimited wants and limited means. More resources bring more wants, and nobody gets more than 24 hours.

review.q: At $2 a gallon, drivers in a town want 50,000 gallons of gas a day and stations can supply 30,000. Which is correct?
choices: Gas is scarce for the first time
Gas is a free good at that price
There is a shortage of 20,000 gallons at $2
There is a shortage of 80,000 gallons at $2
review.why: A shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied at the current price: 50,000 minus 30,000 equals 20,000 gallons. Gas was scarce all along.

review.q: A software company owns its office building, employs 40 programmers and was started by two founders who risked their savings. Which factor of production is missing from that list?
choices: Labor
Capital
Entrepreneurship
Land
review.why: The building is capital, the programmers are labor and the founders are entrepreneurs. Land, meaning natural resources, is not mentioned.

review.q: A farm's output rises from 150 to 180 bushels per acre after it adopts a new seed. What is the percent increase in productivity per acre?
choices: 20 percent
30 percent
16.7 percent
120 percent
review.why: The gain is 30 bushels on a base of 150: 30 divided by 150 equals 0.20, or 20 percent. Dividing by 180 gives the wrong 16.7 percent.

review.q: A country's officials set the number of cars to build, assign workers to the plants and fix the sale price. Which economic system is this?
choices: Market
Command
Traditional
Mixed
review.why: When a central authority answers what, how and for whom by direct order, the system is a command economy.

review.q: Why is the United States described as a mixed economy rather than a pure market economy?
choices: It has both rich and poor households
It uses both dollars and coins
It has both large and small businesses
Private markets produce most goods, but government also provides goods, regulates and taxes
review.why: The mix is between markets and government. Roads, schools, courts and safety rules sit alongside private production.

review.q: A city pays residents $50 for every old refrigerator they turn in, and soon people are buying broken refrigerators at yard sales for $10 to collect the bounty. This shows
choices: a free good
the law of demand
an unintended consequence of an incentive
central planning
review.why: The bounty rewarded turning in refrigerators, not reducing energy use, and people responded to the rule as written.

review.q: Which of these is a normative statement?
choices: Illinois produces more soybeans than most other states
The state should spend more on public universities
A 7-cent bag fee reduced plastic bag use in Chicago
Unemployment rose during the 2020 recession
review.why: Normative statements say what ought to be and rest on values. The word should is the signal. The other three can be checked against evidence.

chapters.title: Opportunity Cost and the Margin
chapters.bigQuestion: When you choose one thing, how do you measure what that choice really cost you?

story.title: The Shift or the Game
story.kicker: A Peoria junior gets two offers for the same Saturday afternoon and has to work out what each one really costs.
paragraphs: Devon works weekends at a hardware store in Peoria for $15 an hour. On Thursday his manager stopped him by the paint counter. A coworker was sick, and could Devon cover a six-hour shift on Saturday, noon to six? That was $90. Devon said he would let her know by Friday. The problem was the calendar on his phone. Saturday at two o'clock, his sister Kiara's basketball team was playing for the conference championship, and on Monday he had already paid $10 for a student ticket.

At lunch he asked his friends. Luis said the choice was easy, because the ticket was already paid for, so the game was basically free. Aaliyah said that was backward. The game was not free at all; it would cost him the whole $90 he could have earned. Luis said she was counting money Devon never had. They argued until the bell, and Devon walked to class more confused than before.

That night he asked his dad. His dad did not answer the question. He asked a different one. If there were no game, what would you do with Saturday afternoon? Devon said he would take the shift, easily. Then that is what the game costs you, his dad said. Not the ticket. The ticket is gone whether you go or not. The game costs you the shift. And the shift costs you the game, which is the last one Kiara plays before she graduates.

Devon had other numbers in his head too. He had $480 saved toward a $1,200 used car, and $90 would move him closer. But he had already worked 14 hours that week, plus practice, plus a chemistry lab report due Monday. The first hours of work each week felt easy. Another six on top of everything else felt different. Was one more shift worth as much as the first one had been?

By Friday afternoon Devon had an answer, and he texted his manager. He had not found a choice without a cost, because there was none. He had found a way to see the cost clearly. This chapter gives you the same tools: opportunity cost, the production possibilities curve, thinking at the margin, ignoring sunk costs, and the reason people specialize and trade.
story.think: Luis says the game is free, and Aaliyah says it costs $90. Who is right, and what should Devon do about the $10 ticket when he decides?

lessons.title: Every Choice Is a Trade-Off
lessons.mainIdea: Because resources are scarce, choosing one option always means giving up others; that exchange is called a trade-off.
reading: It is Friday night, and you have three free hours. You could babysit for a neighbor and earn $45. You could go to a movie with friends for $15. Or you could stay home and sleep. You cannot do all three in the same three hours. Whatever you pick, you give up the rest. Economists call this a *trade-off*: giving up some of one thing to get more of another. Each option you could choose is an *alternative*.

Businesses face trade-offs too. A restaurant with 2,000 square feet must decide how much space goes to tables and how much to the kitchen. More tables mean more customers at once, but a smaller kitchen that cooks more slowly. An Illinois farmer with 500 acres decides how many to plant in corn and how many in soybeans. Every acre planted in corn is an acre not planted in soybeans. The land is fixed, so more of one crop means less of the other.

Governments make the largest trade-offs. Economists often describe a nation's budget as a choice between *guns and butter*: spending on defense versus spending on goods for daily life. A dollar spent on a fighter jet cannot also pay for a school lunch. Trade-offs also involve time. Suppose a pair of shoes costs $5 less at a store 40 minutes away. Driving there trades 40 minutes of your time for $5. That works out to $5 divided by two-thirds of an hour, or $7.50 an hour.

A common mistake is to think a choice has no trade-off because no money changes hands. Staying home to sleep costs nothing in cash, but it still gives up the $45 and the movie. The first step in any smart decision is to list every realistic alternative before choosing. The next lesson shows how to pick out the one alternative that matters most.

words.d: giving up some of one thing in order to get more of something else
one of the possible options you could choose in a decision
a shorthand for a nation's trade-off between spending on defense and spending on everyday goods

look.title: Three Free Hours
look.text: You have three free hours on Friday night. You could babysit and earn $45, see a movie with friends for $15, or finish a history project due Monday. Your friends will be at the movie again next week, but the babysitting offer is only for this Friday.
look.prompt: List the trade-off in each choice. Which option would you pick, and what are you giving up to get it?

check.q: An Illinois farmer has 500 acres and plants 300 in corn. Why is this a trade-off?
choices: The 300 acres of corn cannot also be planted in soybeans
Corn always sells for more than soybeans
The farmer must pay taxes on the corn
The farmer will buy more land next year
check.why: The land is fixed at 500 acres. Every acre used for corn is an acre given up for soybeans, which is what a trade-off means.

check.q: A store 40 minutes away sells the same shoes for $5 less. If you drive there, about what are you earning per hour of your time?
check.why: 40 minutes is two-thirds of an hour. $5 divided by 2/3 equals $7.50 per hour.

check.q: Which statement about trade-offs is correct?
choices: Only choices that cost money involve trade-offs
Choices that use time or space involve trade-offs even when no money is spent
Governments do not face trade-offs because they can raise taxes
Trade-offs disappear when a person has enough income
check.why: Time, space and land are scarce just like money. Using them for one thing means giving up something else.

lessons.title: The Next-Best Alternative
lessons.mainIdea: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best alternative you give up, not a list of everything you did not choose.
reading: Go back to Friday night. Suppose you rank your options: first, the movie; second, babysitting for $45; third, sleeping. If you choose the movie, what did it cost? The *opportunity cost* of a choice is the value of the *next-best alternative* you give up. Here that is the babysitting. It is not the babysitting plus the sleep, because in those three hours you could only have done one of them. Listing every option you skipped is the most common mistake with this idea.

Opportunity cost counts both what you pay and what you give up. The movie ticket is $15. By going, you also give up $45 of babysitting pay. Measured in dollars, the movie costs you $15 plus $45, or $60. That is why a movie can feel cheap to a student with no job offer and expensive to one who turned down paid work for it. The price is the same for both. The opportunity cost is not.

The classic example is college. Suppose a year at a state university has tuition and fees of $12,000 and books of $1,200 (example figures). A student who goes full time also gives up a job that would have paid $30,000. Those lost wages are called *forgone earnings*. The yearly cost of college is $12,000 plus $1,200 plus $30,000, or $43,200. Food and rent are not added, because the student would pay for them either way.

Opportunity cost is personal because each person's next-best alternative is different. A star athlete offered a professional contract gives up far more to attend college than a student with no such offer. None of this says college, or a movie, is a bad choice. It says the choice is worth it only when its benefits are larger than its full opportunity cost. Seeing that cost clearly is the first habit of economic thinking.

words.d: the value of the next-best alternative you give up when you make a choice
the option you would have chosen if your first choice were not available
income you give up by spending time on something other than paid work

look.title: The Same Movie, Two Prices
look.text: Jada and Marcus both go to the same $15 movie on Friday night. Jada had no other plans and would have watched TV at home. Marcus turned down a three-hour shift at a restaurant that pays $14 an hour to go.
look.prompt: What is the opportunity cost of the movie for each of them, in dollars? Why are the two costs different when the ticket price is the same?

check.q: Keisha ranks her Saturday options: 1. a volunteer event, 2. a paid shift worth $60, 3. a nap. She chooses the volunteer event. What is her opportunity cost?
choices: The nap only
The $60 shift and the nap together
Nothing, because volunteering is free
The $60 shift
check.why: Opportunity cost is only the next-best alternative. She could not have done both the shift and the nap in the same time, so the cost is the $60 shift.

check.q: A year of college has $12,000 in tuition and fees, $1,200 in books, and the student gives up a $30,000 job. What is the yearly cost of attending?
check.why: $12,000 plus $1,200 plus $30,000 equals $43,200. Leaving out the forgone earnings gives the wrong $13,200.

check.q: Why are food and rent usually left out of the opportunity cost of college?
choices: They are too small to matter
The government pays for them
The student would pay for them whether or not they attend
They are sunk costs paid before college starts
check.why: Opportunity cost counts only what changes because of the choice. A person must eat and live somewhere either way.

lessons.title: Costs You Pay and Costs You Give Up
lessons.mainIdea: Explicit costs are the money you pay out; implicit costs are the value of what you give up; both count when you judge whether a choice paid off.
reading: Sam spends the summer running a lawn-mowing business in Naperville. He takes in $4,000 from customers. He pays $600 for gas and repairs and $400 to rent a mower. Those payments are *explicit costs*: money actually paid out to someone else. Subtract them from what he took in and Sam's *accounting profit* is $4,000 minus $1,000, or $3,000. On paper, the summer looks like a success.

But Sam had another offer. The city pool wanted him as a lifeguard for the summer at a total of $3,500. By mowing lawns, he gave that up. The value of that lost opportunity is an *implicit cost*: a cost that does not involve paying anyone, but is still real. It is the opportunity cost of using his own time in his own business. Owners often forget it because no bill ever arrives for it.

Economists count both kinds of cost. *Economic profit* is revenue minus explicit costs minus implicit costs. For Sam that is $4,000 minus $1,000 minus $3,500, which equals negative $500. In money terms, Sam would have been $500 better off at the pool. His business earned an accounting profit and an economic loss at the same time. Both numbers are correct; they answer different questions.

Does that mean Sam chose badly? Not necessarily. Maybe he liked being his own boss, or learned skills a lifeguard job would not teach. Those benefits are real even without a price tag. What economic profit does is put the full cost on the table, so Sam can ask whether those other benefits were worth at least $500 to him. That is a much better question than the one the accounting profit answers.

words.d: a cost that involves paying money to someone else, such as rent, wages or supplies
the value of an opportunity given up that involves no payment, such as the wages an owner could earn elsewhere
total revenue minus explicit costs
total revenue minus both explicit and implicit costs

look.title: Sam's Summer Business (example)
look.cite: Made-up figures for one student's summer lawn-mowing business
look.prompt: Which rows are explicit costs and which is an implicit cost? Find the accounting profit and the economic profit. What would the lifeguard pay have to be for economic profit to be zero?

check.q: Using Sam's numbers, what is his accounting profit?
check.why: Accounting profit is revenue minus explicit costs: $4,000 minus $600 minus $400 equals $3,000.

check.q: Which of these is an implicit cost for a person running her own bakery?
choices: The salary she could have earned managing someone else's bakery
The rent she pays for the shop
The flour she buys each week
The wages she pays her helper
check.why: An implicit cost involves no payment. The salary she gives up is the opportunity cost of her own time. The other three are explicit payments.

check.q: A business takes in $50,000, has explicit costs of $30,000, and the owner gave up a $25,000 job. What is its economic profit?
check.why: Economic profit is $50,000 minus $30,000 minus $25,000, which equals negative $5,000, an economic loss.

lessons.title: A Table of Possibilities
lessons.mainIdea: A production possibilities curve shows every combination of two goods an economy can make with all its resources fully used; points on it are efficient.
reading: Imagine a small country that makes only two goods, food and machines. It has a fixed amount of land, workers, tools and know-how. If it puts everything into food, it makes 100,000 tons of food and no machines. If it puts everything into machines, it makes 50,000 machines and no food. Between those extremes lie many mixes. Economists list them in a table and, when they draw them, call the line the *production possibilities curve*, or PPC.

Here is the table for this example, with food in thousands of tons and machines in thousands. Point A: 0 machines, 100 food. Point B: 10 machines, 95 food. Point C: 20 machines, 85 food. Point D: 30 machines, 65 food. Point E: 40 machines, 35 food. Point F: 50 machines, 0 food. Every point in the table uses all of the country's resources. Picture the points on a graph with machines across the bottom and food up the side, joined by a curve that bends outward.

A point on the curve is *efficient*: the country cannot make more of one good without making less of the other. A point inside the curve means resources are being wasted. Suppose the country makes 20 machines and 60 food. Point C shows it could make 20 machines and 85 food, so 25,000 tons of food are being lost. This happens when workers are unemployed or factories sit idle, as in a recession. These are *unemployed resources*.

A point outside the curve is *unattainable* with today's resources and technology. The country cannot make 30 machines and 80 food, because at 30 machines the most food it can make is 65. The PPC turns scarcity into a picture. It shows the limit, the trade-off along that limit, and the waste inside it. It also sets up the next question: why does moving along the curve cost more and more?

words.d: a graph or table showing the combinations of two goods an economy can produce using all its resources
producing the most possible from the resources available, with none wasted
workers, land or machines that are available but not being used to produce anything
describing a combination of goods the economy cannot produce with its current resources and technology

look.title: Food and Machines (example)
look.cite: Made-up production possibilities for a small economy; machines in thousands
look.prompt: Is 40 machines and 30 food efficient, inefficient or unattainable? What about 10 machines and 100 food? Explain each answer using the table.

check.q: Using the table, the country makes 30 machines and 50 food. Which describes this point?
choices: Efficient, because it is on the curve
Unattainable, because it is outside the curve
Inefficient, because 15 more food could be made with 30 machines
Efficient, because it makes some of each good
check.why: At 30 machines the table shows a maximum of 65 food. Making only 50 means 15,000 tons are lost, so the point is inside the curve.

check.q: Which event would most likely move an economy from a point on its PPC to a point inside it?
choices: A recession that leaves many workers unemployed
A new invention that makes farming faster
A decision to make more machines and less food
An increase in the number of workers
check.why: Idle workers are unused resources, so output falls below what the economy could make. The other events either move along the curve or shift it.

check.q: Why is 30 machines and 80 food unattainable in the example?
choices: Because the country prefers food
Because the most food possible with 30 machines is 65
Because 30 machines is more than the country needs
Because all points above 50 food are unattainable
check.why: Point D shows that making 30 machines leaves resources for at most 65 food. Anything beyond that lies outside the curve.

lessons.title: Why the Curve Bows Outward
lessons.mainIdea: Because resources are not equally good at making everything, each extra unit of a good costs more of the other good; this bends the curve outward.
reading: Use the food and machines table to measure the cost of each step. Going from A to B, the country gains 10 machines and gives up 5 food, so each machine costs half a ton of food. From B to C, 10 more machines cost 10 food, or 1 ton each. From C to D, 10 machines cost 20 food, or 2 each. From D to E, they cost 30 food, or 3 each. From E to F, the last 10 machines cost 35 food, or 3.5 each. The more machines the country makes, the more each additional one costs.

This pattern is called the *law of increasing opportunity cost*. The reason is that resources are *specialized*: they are better at some jobs than others. When the country starts making machines, it moves the workers and land best suited to machines and least useful on farms. Little food is lost. But as it keeps going, it must pull in skilled farmers and the richest farmland. Each of those makes few machines and was producing a lot of food.

The increasing cost is what bends the curve outward, away from the origin. If resources were equally good at both jobs, the cost would stay the same at every step and the curve would be a straight line. That is called *constant opportunity cost*. A student splitting study time between two similar subjects might face it: each hour moved from one to the other costs about the same amount of learning in the other.

A common mistake is to read the curve's shape as a statement about what people want. It is not. The PPC shows only what the economy can make. Which point it picks depends on the choices of its people or government. The bow shape tells you something useful for any decision: going all-in on one thing gets expensive, because the last resources you move over are the ones worst suited to it.

words.d: the rule that as production of one good rises, the cost of each extra unit in terms of the other good also rises
workers, land and tools that are much better suited to some kinds of production than to others
a situation in which each extra unit of a good costs the same amount of the other good, giving a straight-line PPC

look.title: Moving the Farmers
look.text: A country decides to double its machine output. The first workers who move from farms to factories are mechanics who worked on tractors. Later the factories need more hands, and the government moves experienced corn growers from the best land in the country into the machine plants.
look.prompt: Which group of workers costs the country more food per machine when they move, and why? Use the idea of specialized resources in your answer.

check.q: In the table, moving from D (30 machines, 65 food) to E (40 machines, 35 food) costs how much food per machine?
choices: 2 tons
0.5 tons
3.5 tons
3 tons
check.why: The country gives up 65 minus 35, or 30 thousand tons of food, for 10 thousand machines. 30 divided by 10 equals 3 tons per machine.

check.q: What causes the law of increasing opportunity cost?
choices: Resources are not equally suited to producing every good
Consumers want more of both goods
Prices rise every year because of inflation
Governments tax the second good more heavily
check.why: The first resources moved are the best fit for the new good. Later ones are worse at it and were more productive where they were, so each unit costs more.

check.q: A PPC is drawn as a straight line. What does that tell you?
choices: The economy is inefficient
The economy is growing
The opportunity cost of each unit stays the same
The economy makes only one good
check.why: A straight line means every step gives up the same amount of the other good, which is constant opportunity cost.

lessons.title: Shifting the Curve Outward
lessons.mainIdea: Economic growth moves the whole curve outward; it comes from more or better resources and technology, and today's choices between capital and consumer goods shape it.
reading: Suppose the country in our example discovers a better way to build machines. With the same workers and land, it can now make 60,000 machines instead of 50,000 if it makes no food, and more machines at every level of food. The whole curve moves outward. Combinations that were unattainable last year are now possible. That outward shift is *economic growth*: an increase in the economy's capacity to produce.

Growth has a few main sources. More resources shift the curve out: more workers, more usable land, more factories. Better technology shifts it out, as when hybrid seed raised corn yields or computers sped up design. More human capital shifts it out, because trained workers produce more in the same hours. A shift can also go inward. A war, a flood or a pandemic that destroys factories or keeps people from working shrinks what the economy can make.

Moving from a point inside the curve to a point on it is not growth. It is putting idle resources back to work. Growth means the limit itself moves. Here is where today's choices matter. *Capital goods* are machines, tools and buildings used to make other things. *Consumer goods* are things people use up directly, like food, clothes and phones. A country that makes more capital goods today gives up some consumption now, but it will have more tools to work with later.

Compare two countries with the same curve this year. Country X chooses 40 percent capital goods and 60 percent consumer goods. Country Y chooses 10 percent capital goods and 90 percent consumer goods. People in Y live better this year. But X is building more factories and equipment, so ten years from now its curve is likely to have moved out much farther. The choice between them is a trade-off between the present and the future, the same one a student makes by studying tonight.

words.d: an increase in an economy's ability to produce goods and services, shown by an outward shift of the PPC
goods such as machines, tools and buildings that are used to produce other goods and services
goods that people buy to use themselves, such as food, clothing and phones

look.title: Two Countries, One Starting Line
look.text: Two countries have identical production possibilities this year. One puts most of its effort into roads, factories, schools and equipment and lives with fewer new consumer goods. The other puts most of its effort into goods people enjoy now, such as clothes, food and entertainment.
look.prompt: Which country's curve is likely to shift out more over ten years, and why? What is the opportunity cost of that growth for the people living there today?

check.q: Which of these would shift a country's PPC outward?
choices: Workers who were unemployed go back to their jobs
A flood destroys several factories
The country decides to make more food and fewer machines
A new technology lets each worker produce more
check.why: Better technology raises the most the economy can make, which moves the curve. Rehiring idle workers moves a point toward the curve but does not move the curve itself.
