check.q: A country moves from a point inside its PPC to a point on it. What happened?
choices: It used resources that had been idle
It grew, because its curve shifted outward
Its opportunity costs fell to zero
It discovered new natural resources
check.why: Moving from inside to on the curve means idle resources went back to work. Growth would require the curve itself to move.

check.q: Why might a country that makes more capital goods today have more consumer goods in the future?
choices: Capital goods are cheaper than consumer goods
Capital goods raise future productive capacity, shifting the curve out
Consumer goods cannot be made in the future
Capital goods are not affected by scarcity
check.why: Machines, factories and tools increase what the economy can produce later. The cost is giving up some consumer goods now.

lessons.title: One More Hour, One More Unit
lessons.mainIdea: Most decisions are about a little more or a little less; keep going as long as the marginal benefit of the next step is at least its marginal cost.
reading: A coffee shop closes at 8 p.m. The owner wonders whether to stay open later. The question is not whether the shop should exist, or whether it is profitable overall. The question is about one more hour. In economics, *marginal* means additional or extra. The *marginal benefit* is what you gain from one more unit of something. The *marginal cost* is what you give up for that one more unit. Comparing the two is called thinking at the margin.

Here are the owner's numbers (example figures). Staying open from 8 to 9 would bring in $120 in extra sales. Staying open from 9 to 10 would add $70. From 10 to 11, only $40. Each extra hour costs $60 for a worker, electricity and supplies. The first extra hour adds $120 and costs $60, so it is worth it. The second adds $70 and costs $60, still worth it by $10. The third adds $40 and costs $60, a $20 loss. The owner should close at 10.

The rule is simple. Keep doing more of something as long as the marginal benefit of the next unit is greater than or equal to its marginal cost, and stop when it falls below. Notice that the owner did not look at the average sales for the whole day. A shop that averages $150 an hour over the day can still lose money in its last hour. Mixing up the average with the marginal is a common and costly mistake.

Thinking at the margin also explains a puzzle that Adam Smith noticed. Water is necessary for life and cheap. Diamonds are not necessary and cost a fortune. The answer is that prices reflect the value of one more unit. Water is so plentiful that one more gallon adds little. Diamonds are so scarce that one more is worth a lot. In the story, Devon's next shift was worth less to him than his first because he had already worked 14 hours that week.

words.d: additional or extra; the next unit of something
the extra benefit gained from one more unit of an activity or good
the extra cost of producing or doing one more unit of something

look.title: Staying Open Late (example)
look.cite: Made-up figures for one coffee shop deciding when to close
look.prompt: Compare each hour's extra sales with its cost. What time should the shop close? If the cost of each extra hour rose to $80, when should it close?

check.q: Extra sales are $120, $70 and $40 for three extra hours, and each hour costs $60. How many extra hours should the shop stay open?
check.why: The first two hours bring in more than their $60 cost. The third brings in $40, less than $60, so the shop should stop after two extra hours.

check.q: Why can a shop that averages $150 in sales per hour still lose money in its last hour?
choices: Average sales are always lower than marginal sales
The average counts only the last hour
The last hour's sales can be far lower than the average
Marginal cost is always zero at night
check.why: The decision about one more hour depends on that hour's sales and cost, not the day's average. Busy hours can hide a slow final hour.

check.q: Why do diamonds cost more than water even though water is more necessary?
choices: Water is produced by the government
Diamonds have a higher total usefulness than water
Water has no opportunity cost
One more diamond is worth much more than one more gallon of plentiful water
check.why: Prices reflect marginal value. Water is plentiful, so an extra gallon adds little. Diamonds are scarce, so an extra one adds a lot.

lessons.title: Sunk Costs Stay Sunk
lessons.mainIdea: A sunk cost has already been paid and cannot be recovered, so it should not affect a decision about what to do next.
reading: You paid $60 for a concert ticket that cannot be refunded or resold. On the night of the show you have a bad cold, it is pouring rain, and a friend invites you to a quiet movie night at her house. Many people drag themselves to the concert anyway, saying they cannot waste $60. But the $60 is gone whether you go or not. It is a *sunk cost*: money, time or effort already spent that cannot be gotten back.

The only question that matters is about the future. Which will you enjoy more tonight, the concert with a cold in the rain or the movie night? Compare only the costs and benefits that still depend on your choice. Economists call those *relevant costs*. The ticket price is not one of them, because nothing you do tonight changes it. In the story, Devon's $10 basketball ticket was sunk too. His real choice was between the game and the $90 shift.

Businesses make the same mistake on a larger scale. Suppose a company has spent $2 million building a new app. Finishing it will take another $1 million, and the company now expects it to earn only $800,000 in sales. Managers who think about the $2 million already spent may push ahead to avoid wasting it. But the $2 million is sunk. Going forward, spending $1 million to earn $800,000 loses $200,000. The right move is to stop.

Letting a sunk cost drive a choice is called the *sunk cost fallacy*. It keeps people in bad investments, failing projects and even classes or teams they no longer want. Ignoring sunk costs is not the same as ignoring lessons. The money spent can teach you something for next time. It just cannot be recovered by spending more. Good decisions look forward, not back.

words.d: a cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, whatever you decide next
a cost that will change depending on which choice you make, and so should affect the decision
the mistake of continuing something because of what you already spent on it rather than what lies ahead

look.title: Halfway Through the Season
look.text: Rosa paid a $150 nonrefundable fee to join a club volleyball team. Six weeks in, she dreads every practice, and a local restaurant has offered her a job on practice nights paying $12 an hour for 6 hours a week. The season has eight weeks left.
look.prompt: Should the $150 fee affect her choice? List the relevant costs and benefits of staying on the team for the last eight weeks.

check.q: A company has spent $2 million on a project. Finishing costs $1 million more and will bring in $800,000. What should it do?
choices: Finish, so the $2 million is not wasted
Stop, because the extra $1 million will earn back only $800,000
Finish, because $800,000 is a lot of money
Spend more to make the project bigger
check.why: The $2 million is sunk. Looking forward, spending $1 million to earn $800,000 loses $200,000, so stopping is the better choice.

check.q: Which of these is a sunk cost?
choices: A nonrefundable deposit already paid for a trip
The cost of gas for a trip you have not taken yet
Wages you would earn if you skip the trip
The price of a hotel you have not booked
check.why: The deposit is already paid and cannot come back. The others still depend on what you choose, so they are relevant costs.

check.q: Devon paid $10 for a game ticket and was offered a $90 shift at the same time. What should he compare when deciding?
choices: The $10 ticket and the $90 shift
Only the $10 ticket
The value of the game to him and the $90 shift
The $90 shift minus the $10 ticket
check.why: The $10 is sunk whether he goes or not. The live choice is between the value of watching the game and the $90 of pay.

lessons.title: Weighing a Real Decision
lessons.mainIdea: Cost-benefit analysis lists every cost, including opportunity costs, and every benefit of a choice, puts dollar values on what it can, and compares them.
reading: Jordan is a junior deciding whether to take a college course at a community college this summer. The class meets weekday mornings for six weeks. He could work those same hours at a grocery store. To decide, he uses *cost-benefit analysis*: a step-by-step way to weigh a choice. Step one, name the options. Step two, list every cost, including opportunity costs. Step three, list every benefit. Step four, put dollar values on what you can and compare.

The costs, with example figures: tuition of $450 and books of $100, which are explicit. He also gives up 10 hours of work a week for 6 weeks, or 60 hours, at $15 an hour. That is $900 of forgone earnings, an implicit cost. Total cost: $450 plus $100 plus $900, or $1,450. The main benefit: the three credits will transfer to the state university he plans to attend, where the same course would cost about $1,500 in tuition.

Compare. Benefits of about $1,500 minus costs of $1,450 give a *net benefit* of $50. In money terms the class barely wins. That is where the benefits without a price tag come in. Jordan gets a taste of college work, a line on his applications and a lighter load as a freshman. Against that, he loses summer free time and six weeks of work experience. These are *nonmonetary* costs and benefits: real, but hard to put in dollars.

Cost-benefit analysis does not make the decision for you. When the numbers are close, as here, your own values decide. When they are far apart, the numbers usually settle it. Its real power is making you count what people forget: forgone wages, time and the next-best alternative. Governments use the same method, on a bigger scale, when they decide whether a new highway or a flood wall is worth what it costs.

words.d: a method of making a decision by listing and comparing all the costs and benefits of each option
total benefits minus total costs
describing a cost or benefit that is real but not easily measured in money, such as time, stress or experience

look.title: Jordan's Summer Class (example)
look.cite: Made-up figures for one student's summer course decision
look.prompt: Which rows are costs and which is a benefit? Find the net benefit. If Jordan's job paid $20 an hour instead, would the class still come out ahead in money terms?

check.q: Jordan gives up 60 hours of work at $15 an hour. What is his forgone income?
check.why: 60 hours times $15 per hour equals $900. That is an implicit cost of taking the class.

check.q: Total costs are $1,450 and total money benefits are $1,500. What is the net benefit?
check.why: Net benefit is benefits minus costs: $1,500 minus $1,450 equals $50.

check.q: Which item would Jordan list as a nonmonetary benefit of the class?
choices: The $450 tuition
The $900 in wages
Getting used to college-level work
The $1,500 saved at the university
check.why: Experience with college work is a real benefit, but it has no price tag. The other items are measured in dollars.

lessons.title: Why People Specialize
lessons.mainIdea: People and places gain by specializing in what they do at the lowest opportunity cost, even when someone else is better at everything.
reading: Ana and Ben share an apartment and have two hours on Sunday to make sandwiches for the week and fold laundry. In one hour Ana can make 6 sandwiches or fold 12 shirts. Ben can make 2 sandwiches or fold 8 shirts. Ana is faster at both jobs. When a person can produce more of something with the same time, she has an *absolute advantage* in it. Ana has an absolute advantage in both. Does that mean she should do everything?

Look at opportunity cost. For Ana, one sandwich costs 2 shirts, because 12 shirts divided by 6 sandwiches is 2. For Ben, one sandwich costs 4 shirts, because 8 divided by 2 is 4. Ana gives up less to make a sandwich, so she has the *comparative advantage* in sandwiches: the lower opportunity cost. For shirts it flips. One shirt costs Ana half a sandwich, but costs Ben only a quarter of one. Ben has the comparative advantage in folding shirts.

Now compare two plans. If each spends one hour on each job, Ana makes 6 sandwiches and 12 shirts, and Ben makes 2 sandwiches and 8 shirts. Together: 8 sandwiches and 20 shirts. If they *specialize*, Ben folds for both hours, making 16 shirts. Ana makes sandwiches for 90 minutes, which is 9, and folds for 30 minutes, which is 6 shirts. Together: 9 sandwiches and 22 shirts. Same people, same two hours, more of both. That extra output is the gain from *specialization*.

Adam Smith saw the same thing in a pin workshop. He described ten workers who split pin-making into separate steps and together made more than 48,000 pins a day, while one person doing every step alone could hardly make twenty. Splitting a job into steps done by different people is the *division of labor*. It is why a Chicago hospital has surgeons, nurses and billing clerks rather than doctors who do everything. Unit 18 returns to comparative advantage between whole countries.

words.d: the ability to produce more of a good than someone else using the same amount of time or resources
the ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than someone else
focusing on producing a narrow range of goods or tasks instead of doing everything yourself
splitting the work of making something into separate steps done by different workers

look.title: Smith on the Division of Labor
look.text: The greatest improvement in the productive powers of labour, and the greater part of the skill, dexterity, and judgment with which it is any where directed, or applied, seem to have been the effects of the division of labour.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 1, 1776
look.prompt: Smith says dividing work raises both output and skill. How does doing one step over and over make a worker more skilled? Give an example from a job you know.

check.q: In one hour Ana makes 6 sandwiches or folds 12 shirts. What is her opportunity cost of one sandwich?
choices: 6 shirts
0.5 shirts
12 shirts
2 shirts
check.why: In the time it takes to make 6 sandwiches she could fold 12 shirts. 12 divided by 6 equals 2 shirts per sandwich.

check.q: Ana is faster than Ben at both jobs. Why should Ben still fold the shirts?
choices: Ben has the lower opportunity cost for folding shirts
Ben has an absolute advantage in folding
Ana should do both jobs because she is faster
Folding shirts has no opportunity cost
check.why: A shirt costs Ben a quarter of a sandwich and Ana half of one. Ben gives up less, so he has the comparative advantage in folding.

check.q: Without specializing, Ana and Ben make 8 sandwiches and 20 shirts. With specializing, they make 9 and 22. What is the gain?
choices: 2 sandwiches and 1 shirt
1 sandwich and 2 shirts
17 sandwiches and 42 shirts
No gain, because they worked the same hours
check.why: 9 minus 8 is 1 extra sandwich, and 22 minus 20 is 2 extra shirts, from the same two hours of work each.

lessons.title: Trade Makes Both Sides Better Off
lessons.mainIdea: In a voluntary trade both sides expect to gain, because each values what it gets more than what it gives up; trade creates value rather than just moving it.
reading: You buy an iced coffee for $4. You would have paid up to $6 for it on a hot afternoon, so you walk away feeling $2 better off. The shop's cost to make it, counting milk, ice, cup and the worker's time, is $3, so it is $1 better off. Nobody was tricked. Each side gave up something it valued less for something it valued more. That is why a *voluntary exchange* happens at all. Together, the two sides are $3 better off than before.

This means trade is not a *zero-sum* game, where one side's gain is exactly the other's loss. A poker pot is zero-sum: whatever one player wins, the others lose. A voluntary trade is positive-sum. Value is created because the coffee moved from someone who valued it at $3 to someone who valued it at $6. The extra satisfaction both sides get is called the *gains from trade*.

Specialization only works because of trade. Ana makes sandwiches and Ben folds shirts, and then they share. Illinois farmers grow corn and soybeans far beyond what they could eat, then sell the crop and buy trucks, phones and medicine. Chicago became a trading center for exactly this reason. The Chicago Board of Trade, founded in 1848, gave farmers and grain buyers one place to meet and agree on prices. Specializing and trading make people dependent on each other, a condition called *interdependence*.

Trade does not help everyone equally, and later chapters look at who wins and who loses when it grows. A trade can also go wrong when one side is lied to or forced, which is why laws against fraud matter. But the core idea holds. When two people agree freely to a trade, both expect to be better off, or they would say no. That simple fact, repeated millions of times a day, is the engine of a market economy.

words.d: a trade that both sides agree to because each expects to be better off
describing a situation in which one side's gain is exactly equal to the other side's loss
the extra value both sides receive when they trade instead of producing everything themselves
the condition of people and places relying on each other for goods and services

look.title: The Used Bike
look.text: Mia has a used bike she no longer rides. She would sell it for anything above $80. Theo needs a bike to get to his summer job and would pay up to $150. They agree on a price of $110.
look.prompt: How much better off is Mia? How much better off is Theo? What is the total value created by the trade, and why did it happen without anyone forcing it?

check.q: A buyer values a coffee at $6 and pays $4. The shop's cost is $3. What is the total gain from the trade?
check.why: The buyer gains $6 minus $4, or $2. The shop gains $4 minus $3, or $1. Together they gain $3.

check.q: Why is a voluntary trade not a zero-sum game?
choices: Both sides expect to end up better off, so value is created
The seller always gains and the buyer always loses
The government makes sure the gains are equal
Prices never change after the trade
check.why: Each side gives up something it values less for something it values more, so both can gain at once.

check.q: Illinois farmers grow far more corn than they can use and sell it to buy other goods. This shows
choices: a command economy
a zero-sum game
specialization combined with trade
the sunk cost fallacy
check.why: The farmers specialize in what they do well, then trade the surplus for goods others make. That is specialization and trade together.

lessons.title: Investing in Your Own Skills
lessons.mainIdea: Education and training cost tuition plus the pay you give up, and they can raise what you earn for years; weigh the full cost against the expected gain.
reading: Maya is 18 and earns $25,000 a year at a warehouse (all numbers in this lesson are examples). She is thinking about a one-year welding certificate at a community college. Tuition and gear cost $7,000. She would work less during the program and lose about $15,000 in pay. So the full cost is $7,000 + $15,000 = $22,000. The pay she gives up is an opportunity cost, and it is often bigger than the tuition.

Now the benefit. Suppose certified welders near Maya start at $37,000 a year. That is $12,000 more than her warehouse job. Divide the cost by the yearly gain: $22,000 / $12,000 is about 1.8. After about two years of work, the certificate has paid for itself. Every year after that is extra income. Economists call the skills and knowledge a person builds *human capital*, because like a machine it costs money now and pays off later.

There are many paths. A four-year degree costs more and takes longer, but on average it leads to higher pay over a career. An *apprenticeship* lets a person earn a wage while learning a trade, such as electrician or plumber, so the opportunity cost is small. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show every year that workers with more education earn more on average and are unemployed less often. Averages do not decide for any one person, though.

A good decision weighs more than the average. How long will the program take? Will you borrow, and at what interest rate? Do jobs in that field exist where you want to live? Will you finish? A common mistake is to count only tuition and forget the lost pay. Another is to assume a credential guarantees a raise. The *return on investment* is the gain compared with the full cost, and it differs from person to person.

words.d: the skills, knowledge and training a person has that let them produce more and earn more
a training program in which a person earns a wage while learning a trade on the job
the gain from an investment compared with its full cost

look.prompt: How much more does welding pay each year than the current job? About how many years does it take to earn back its full cost?

check.q: A one-year program costs $6,000 in tuition. During it, you give up a job that pays $24,000 a year. What is the full cost of the program?
check.why: Full cost = tuition + the pay you give up: $6,000 + $24,000 = $30,000.

check.q: A training program's full cost is $40,000. It raises yearly pay by $10,000. About how many years of work does it take to earn the cost back?
choices: 10 years
40 years
4 years
2 years
check.why: $40,000 / $10,000 per year = 4 years; after that, the extra pay is a gain.

check.q: Which choice is an investment in human capital?
choices: Buying a newer car
Taking a longer vacation
Upgrading a phone plan
Earning an electrician's license through an apprenticeship
check.why: Human capital is skill and knowledge; an apprenticeship builds a trade skill that raises future earnings.

review.q: Priya can go to a party, work a $50 shift, or study, and she ranks them in that order. She goes to the party. What is her opportunity cost?
choices: The $50 shift
The shift and studying
Studying only
Nothing, since she enjoyed the party
review.why: Opportunity cost is the single next-best alternative. Her second choice was the $50 shift.

review.q: A business takes in $80,000. It pays $50,000 in rent, wages and supplies, and the owner gave up a $40,000 job. Which is correct?
choices: Accounting profit $30,000 and economic profit $30,000
Accounting profit $30,000 and economic profit -$10,000
Accounting profit -$10,000 and economic profit $30,000
Accounting profit $80,000 and economic profit $40,000
review.why: Accounting profit is $80,000 minus $50,000, or $30,000. Subtracting the $40,000 implicit cost as well gives an economic loss of $10,000.

review.q: On a PPC, moving from 20 to 30 machines lowers food from 85 to 65 units. What is the opportunity cost of each of those 10 machines?
choices: 20 units of food
10 units of food
2 units of food
0.5 units of food
review.why: 20 units of food are given up for 10 machines. 20 divided by 10 equals 2 units of food per machine.

review.q: Which of these would shift a country's production possibilities curve inward?
choices: A rise in the number of trained workers
A move from one point on the curve to another
A decision to produce more capital goods
An earthquake that destroys many factories
review.why: Destroying factories reduces the resources available, so the most the economy can make falls. The other choices keep or expand capacity.

review.q: A tutor charges $20 an hour. For you, a first hour of tutoring before a test is worth $50, a second $25 and a third $15. How many hours should you buy?
review.why: Buy hours while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost. The first two hours are worth more than $20; the third is worth only $15.

review.q: You paid $200 for a nonrefundable course. Halfway through, you realize it is not useful and a paid internship is available on the same days. What should you do about the $200?
choices: Finish the course so the $200 is not wasted
Ignore it and compare the rest of the course with the internship
Add it to the value of the internship
Ask for twice as much pay at the internship
review.why: The $200 is a sunk cost. Only the costs and benefits still ahead should decide the choice.

review.q: In an hour, Lena can paint 4 signs or bake 8 pies. Omar can paint 3 signs or bake 3 pies. Who has the comparative advantage in painting signs?
choices: Lena, because she paints more signs per hour
Neither, because they paint at similar speeds
Both of them equally
Omar, because a sign costs him 1 pie while it costs Lena 2 pies
review.why: For Lena a sign costs 8 divided by 4, or 2 pies. For Omar it costs 3 divided by 3, or 1 pie. Omar gives up less, so he has the comparative advantage.

review.q: Mia would sell her bike for anything above $80, and Theo would pay up to $150. They agree on $110. What are the total gains from trade?
review.why: Mia gains $110 minus $80, or $30. Theo gains $150 minus $110, or $40. Together that is $70, the gap between $150 and $80.
